THE GAMMA, ITS FOUNDING AND
NOTES ON ITS HISTORY
By Richard M. Howland, Gamma '38
ON
THE 18th of September,
1821, in the parish church in
Amherst, Massachusetts, a group of
townspeople and clergymen gath
ered together to dedicate a new col
lege. Noah Webster, president of the
board, presided and the Rev. Dr.
Leland preached from the text, "On
this rock will I build my church, and
the gates of hell shall not prevail
against it."
That the "gates of hell did not
prevail" against Amherst College in
the early years of its infancy may
doubtless be laid to the tireless de
votion and the unremitting labor
bestowed by its early sons and bene
factors. From the tenure of Zephan
iah Swift Moore, the first president,
virtually up to Civil War days Am
herst fought for an existence against
bankruptcy; internal dissension; and
the bitter animosity of the Massa
chusetts Legislature, which refused
to incorporate the college, chiefly on
the grounds that two colleges (Har
vard and Williams) were sufficient
provision for the education of the
youth of the state. But the religious
dedication and determination of the
men of Amherst was not to be de
nied, and the legislature finally in
corporated the college in 1825.
This disposed of one problem. The
others remained. Sixteen years lat
ter, in September, 1841, when the
Gamma chapter of Psi Upsilon first
made its appearance on the campus,
the college, says William S. Tyler in
his History of Amherst College, "con
tinued to flounder and sink deeper
in the mire." The Gamma and its
senior Amherst secret society, Alpha
Delta Phi, met and prevailed over
bitter opposition to Greek letter so
cieties which undoubtedly added
much to the internecine warfare
which almost succeeded in tearing
the college apart.
The survival of F^si U at Amherst
is not extraordinary in the light of
the boyish exuberance and zeal
shown by the early Gammies. This
is well demonstrated in the oftquoted letter of William E. Robin
son, Beta 1841, who instituted the
Gamma and wrote of the historic
founding :
"When Edward Trask (Delta '40)
and I, in 1841, instituted the Am
herst chapter, I took with me some
thirteen or fifteen badges made at
Albany. Trask's mother lived in
Springfield, whence we drove to Am
herst with two of her spirited steeds,
making quite a display as we arrived
at the hotel of the quiet collegiate
town. The next day we enjoyed from
the gallery the excitement caused in
the chapel, at public exercises, by
the entrance of our new boys, the
flashes of light that gleamed from
their badges being reflected by those
which flamed from our own. It was
a grand day for the Delta, Beta and
Gamma, especially for the Gamma."
Today the Gammy (Gamma) can
look back on a history which is more
than impressive. Always to be reck
oned as a leader on the campus, even

142 the diamond of psi upsilon
in the years when the chapter was at
its weakest by contemporary stand
ards, it has given Amherst a large
number of its most famous sons : and
of those who have not become so
famous, the Gammies as a group
stand out as the most actively loyal.
At reunions the Gammies are most
in evidence, and the Hall of the
Gamma is usually unofficial reunion
headquarters for singing.
To mention a few of the Gammy
illustrious (the list does not pretend
to be complete, and grievous omis
sions must be excused on the ground
of shameful and youthful ignorance)
Julius H. Seelye, '49, fifth President
of Amherst College; Edwin A. Gros
venor, '67, beloved Professor of Am
herst and devoted Brother of the
Gamma; his son, Gilbert H. Gros
venor, '97, President of the National
Geographic Society; Robert Lan
sing, '86, Secretary of State under
President Wilson; Joseph B. East
man, '04, Chairman of the Inter
state Commerce Commission; Al
bert E. Stearns, '94, former Head
Master of Phillips Academy Andover
and now Chairman of the Board of
Trustees of Amherst; William S.
Clark, '48, President of Massachu
setts Agricultural College.
There are countless brothers, who
while making a name for themselves
in the business and professional
world, have made Amherst College
and the Gamma a
devotionally per
sonal vocation. Among those who
have passed on are Mason W. Tyler
and M. F. Dickinson of the class of
'62; G. Henry Whitcomb, '64; Her
bert L. Bridgman, '66, who for many
years was the President of the Psi U
Fraternity: Judge Henry P. Field,
'80; and Eugene S. Wilson, '02. Of
those still active are Rev. Sherrod
Soule, '85; Oliver B. Merrill, '91,
Frederick S. Allis, '93, for many
years Secretary of the Alumni Coun
cil, and his successor, E. S. Wilson,
Jr., '29, Frederick S. Fales, '96, Hugh
H. Weed, '05, Frederich S. Bale, '06,
Thomas C. Heisey, '08, William C.
Esty, '16, may be mentioned as rep
resentative samples.
Along pedagogic lines the list is no
less impressive; the "Who's Who"
of Amherst faculty members has an
auspicious Gammy flavor; and Gam
mies have made no less a mark in
other learned institutions.
The college�
and the Gammy
with it�
has grown and prospered
in the past century; but the town of
Amherst is still (with modern im
provements) the "quiet collegiate
town" it was in Robinson's day. The
Gamma started the building of new
fraternity houses at Amherst which,
followed by all the others, has made
Amherst one of the most beautiful
of all college towns. The Psi U house
dominates the long, green village
common, shaded by elms and sur
rounded by beautiful fraternity
houses, college buildings and the
long, rambling Lord Jeffrey Inn.
This quiet common has been a haven
for countless world-weary Amherst
alumni who take their vacations in
winter or summer, spring or fall,
driving out through the Holyoke
Range, dining at Northampton's old
Wiggin's Tavern, stopping for "re
freshment" at old Dick Rahar's Inn,
sitting by the open fireplace in the
Lord Jeff, or, in all seasons but
winter, sitting placidly in the sun,
chair tilted i back, basking in the
quiet calm of Amherst.

THE ROYSTERS IN SHANGHAI
October 2, 1940
Dear Brothers :
I
FEEL that we who are far away
should report home once in a
while.
Thanks for sending me The Dia
mond, which is coming to Shanghai
regularly now.
I can report that I am married
now, having been joined with the
former Miss Grace Preston Naylor
of Hartford, Connecticut. We are
making our home in the American
Club here in Shanghai. Have not
met any Psi U's in Shanghai. Do
you know of any here.? Most of the
M. A.'s and Ph. D's hereabouts,
from Columbia, and from other
American Universities, are . . . alas
. . . Chinese. Was recently invited
to a dinner of the local graduates of
the Uiiiversity of Pennsylvania.
Eighty per cent of those present were
Chinese men and women.
Am local manager of Pemberton
& Penn Federal Inc., U.S.A., an
American Leaf Tobacco firm. Busi
ness is better than fair. Am learning
Chinese, and can
carry on a simple
conversation in polished (?) Manda
rin. It is more difficult than French.
Was in Hongkong recently, and
everything was under control. Was
also in Japan . . .
Nagasaki, Kobe,
Osaka, Yokohama, Tokyo . . . and
everything was quiet. Shanghai is,
of course, a powder box . . .
armed
to the teeth and expecting trouble.
Sometimes, we Americans get to
gether of an
evening, and . . . drink
a toast to the President of the
United States. It gives us
strength.
I was with several high class Chinese
the other evening; proposed a toast
to the President of the United States.
It was a thrill to see those Chinese
gentlemen snap to attention and
drink that toast with moist eyes.
What are we doing, and what can
we do, to keep and merit that pro
found respect? I hope we never take
it for granted.
Yours in the Brotherhoodj

THE JUSTICE OF MORALITY AND
HALF-WAY MEASURES
By James Angell McLaughlin, Phi '12
Harvard University Law School
Published in the New York Times, Jan, 26, 191^1
THE
state of American public
opinion as crystallized by the
President's recent speeches repre
sents an acceptance of certain im
portant points.
1. The United States is not to be
locked behind a Chinese wall either
by its foreign enemies or by its own
isolationists.
2. The strength of the British
fleet in the Atlantic has been a
friendly strength. Isolationism is an
illusion which can no longer be in
dulged when that friendly strength
is seriously challenged.
3. A new order of tyranny seeks
to spread over every continent today.
4. We have learned much from
the lesson of Norway and others.
5. The future of all American Re
publics is today in serious danger.
The need of the moment is that our
actions and our policy should be
devoted to meeting this danger.
6. Our enemies are known and
named: Germany, Japan, Italy.
Those nations who have the power
and the will to struggle actively
against our enemies gain us time for
our own defense. They become (or
remain) our particular friends. They
are known and named: England,
China, Greece.
7. Our national policy has been
based on a decent respect for the
rights and dignity of all nations
large and small.
8. The justice of morality must
and will win in the end.
And what conclusion has Ameri
can public opinion so far accepted.''
James A. McLaughlin, Phi '12
For us, no Chinese wall.
1. That we must act as the great
arsenal of democracy. 2. That we
should avoid personal risk to our
citizens (as long as may be).
It is submitted that the foregoing
eight points call for conclusions less
timid. The result is much the same
whether the conclusions are tested

146 the diamond of psi upsilon
on a practical or on an ethical basis.
Many of my friends who are not
personally immune to ethical con
siderations tell me that the Ameri
can people can be brought to face
the world only by appealing to their
fears and to their immediate ma
terial interests. I wonder if this does
our people justice.'*
In any event, would it not be
proper to examine our course with
somewhat more attention to its ethi
cal aspects.? We have heard much
lately of "war hysteria" and some
what less of hysterical inhibitions
about facing facts. We prepare de
liberately to devote our main ener
gies to forging deadly weapons and
to give Siich weapons to others for
immeidiate use. We should not do
thisjifwe believe that both sides of
all wars are always wrong. We
should not do this unless we believe
that one side is right as we have been
permitted to see the right. In any
event, we now propose to abandon
the idea of arming both sides for our
own profit and we take sides with a
view to deciding the war in the only
manner consistent with the main
tenance of the civilization to which
we have become accustomed. At
this stage we can no longer deceive
ourselves with talk about neutrality.
The Nazis' disregard of internation
al law has rendered it inoperative
as a legalistic concept. As an ethical
matter, we do not find ourselves
neutral in a struggle whose issues
our President has fairly described.
We hear much talk of rights and
interests these days, but if we begin
to consider what the President well
calls "the justice of morality" we

crash on

ment�

cently.

shall be hard put to maintain. This month,
however, two of the brothers have been called
up for active service. Both will go overseas
within the year. Brother Alley has a lieu
tenant's commission in the Queen's Own
Rifles, crack Toronto regiment; Brother Reid
will serve in the tank division of the recently
motorized Governor-General's Horse Guards.
Meanwhile Brothers Brown, Allen, Linton
and Smith, all students of engineering, are
harassed by tests which allow them to gradu
ate in a month's time. In vital industries
there is sore need for trained men. Consesequently they are being released ahead of
schedule by the university.
Scarcely less belligerent than those serving
under the Crown are the chapter's hockey
stars. Recently the sport columnist for the
Toronto Globe and Mail devoted his space to
lofty paeans in praise of Brother George
McNamara. The column was a string of un
qualified superlatives such as "the best stickhandler since�
you name when." It men
tioned that George had received offers from
Jack Adams of the Detroit Red Wings which
if accepted would make him the highest paid
rookie in professional hockey. The columnist
commiserated with Mr. Adams over
George's
refusal, added the philosophic balm, "there
are some things which money cannot buy."
And while on the subject it would be criminal
oversight to ignore the hockey prowess that
Brothers Paul McNamara and Claude Morri
son are winning with their mercurial blades.
Brother Jack Muir reached the quarter
finals in a tournament for the Ontario bad
minton championship: our tears are shed for
this adept whose great battle is remembered
in the far reaches of British Columbia. But
the tears mingle with congratulatory smiles
to graduate Brother Rod Phelan who on the
day of this writing smashed the shuttlecock
to championship and is now kneeling for the
boys.
Donald Rohr

ZETA ZETA
University of British Columbia
This spring finds the Zeta Zeta transferring
most of its time for extracurricular activity
to military training. At Christmas time many
passed their Common to AU Arms examina
tion, leading to qualifications for a commis
sion. Each brother is willing and determined
to bear his share in the War.
Brothers Moodie and Sturdy, president
and secretary, respectively, of the Interfra
ternity Council at U.B.C., after several
months' hard work in arranging the Interna
tional Interfraternity Red Cross Ball, were
rewarded for their efforts with an outstanding
success. Approximately $2,000 was netted for
the Red Cross Fund on this campus. Many
brothers were present.
On February 8 the Mothers' Club and the
active chapter were joint hosts at a tea at the
fraternity house. The splendid attendance of
alumni and active brothers & their parents
exemplified the great interest held for the
Zeta Zeta by all those connected with it.
The annual Spring Formal was held in the -
Windsor Room of the Hotel Georgia on the
evening of February 14.
The curtailment of athletics on the campus
has given added impetus to interfraternity
sports. In rugby, basketbaU, and table-tennis
Zeta Zeta has remained undefeated.
Brothers Gerry White and Stan Beale
have recently left the campus. The former
joins Brothers Kenmuir and Sweetman in the
R.C.A.F., the latter has entered private busi
ness.
